Cartesian.childMeaning: Using a grid of numbered axes to give a position.
practiceSentences: Cartesian coordinates give every point a pair of numbers.
Which Cartesian quadrant is this point in?
The Cartesian plane has an x axis and a y axis crossing at zero.
She plotted the results on Cartesian axes.
Cartesian is named after Descartes, which is why it keeps its capital.

abiotic.childMeaning: To do with the non-living parts of an environment.
practiceSentences: Temperature, light and soil are abiotic factors.
Which abiotic factor limits growth on this slope?
An abiotic factor shapes what can live somewhere at all.
The survey recorded abiotic conditions before counting a single species.
Abiotic means non-living; biotic means living.

accumulation.childMeaning: A gradual gathering of something into a larger amount.
practiceSentences: An accumulation of small savings paid for the whole journey.
What accumulation of evidence changed her mind?
History is an accumulation of ordinary days as well as famous ones.
The accumulation of dust on the trunk showed how long it had stood there.
Accumulation is slow, which is why it goes unnoticed.

accuracy.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept - it is plain enough for this grade.
practiceSentences: The accuracy of the family record surprised the archivist.
How would you test the accuracy of this account?
Accuracy matters more than fluency in a translation.
She checked the dates twice for accuracy.
Accuracy is being right; precision is being exact.

activism.note: Meaning inherited from grade 6 and kept.
practiceSentences: Her activism began with a letter to the local paper.
What activism has changed a law you benefit from?
Activism is patient work that occasionally looks sudden.
Online activism reaches further and commits less.
Activism seeks change; reporting seeks to describe it.

administration.note: Sentence 4 named Teacher Yasmin, who belongs to Grade 5 and is not in this grade's readings - and the set held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: Why did the administration announce the cancellation so suddenly?
The administration met to discuss safety before the storm arrived.
Please listen carefully, everyone, the administration has an important announcement!
Imani passed the administration's message on to the whole class.
Administration is the running of a thing, and also the people who run it.

adolescence.childMeaning: The years between childhood and adulthood.
practiceSentences: Adolescence is when identity stops being inherited and starts being chosen.
How long does adolescence last?
Adolescence is a stage, not a problem to be solved.
She wrote about her adolescence without embarrassment.
Adolescence differs between cultures more than biology suggests.

advancement.childMeaning: Movement forward, in a career or in knowledge.
practiceSentences: Her advancement to head of the archive took eleven years.
What advancement did the century bring to ordinary families?
Advancement is not the same as change.
The advancement of medicine altered how long a life lasts.
Advancement suggests a direction; progress suggests a value.

affiliation.note: All four inherited sentences were about SPORT - a registered club, the athletics team, a county championship - which is unit 6's subject. On a card in the unit about family and identity, affiliation is which groups a person belongs to. The set also held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: Her strongest affiliation was to the village she had left as a child.
What affiliation shapes your sense of who you are?
An affiliation can be inherited, chosen, or quietly dropped.
Sana listed three affiliations and said the last one mattered most.
Affiliation is belonging that can be named.

algebraic.childMeaning: Using letters to stand for numbers in a rule or formula.
practiceSentences: The algebraic expression works for every value of n.
Which algebraic rule describes this pattern?
An algebraic statement says something about all numbers at once.
She wrote the algebraic form and the pattern became obvious.
Algebraic uses letters; arithmetic uses only numbers.

allocation.note: Sentences 1 and 5 were the same sentence - 'The council said they were opposed to the unfair allocation of tasks.' and 'We are opposed to unfair allocation of tasks.' - and sentence 3 named Dina, who belongs to Grade 6 and is not in this grade's readings.
practiceSentences: The council opposed the unfair allocation of tasks.
Is the allocation of duties fair across every form?
Zara argued that the allocation gave one group far too much work.
The board promised to review the allocation before the new term.
An allocation is a decision about shares, and someone always makes it.

allusion.childMeaning: An indirect reference to another work, person or event.
practiceSentences: The title is an allusion to an older poem.
Which allusion opens the second stanza?
An allusion rewards the reader who recognises it and does not punish the one who does not.
The speech was full of allusions to the founding story.
An allusion hints at something; a quotation states it.

altruism.childMeaning: Acting for others' good without expecting a return.
practiceSentences: Altruism built the footbridge before the council funded it.
Is altruism ever entirely free of self-interest?
Altruism costs the giver something, or it is only kindness.
Her altruism was quiet and completely reliable.
Altruism gives without expecting; generosity may still enjoy the thanks.

ambiguity.childMeaning: The state of having more than one possible meaning.
practiceSentences: The ambiguity in the invitation left everyone guessing the dress code.
Where does the ambiguity in this line come from?
Ambiguity is a fault in a contract and a resource in a poem.
She removed the ambiguity by naming the date outright.
Ambiguity is not the same as vagueness: it offers two clear readings, not none.

ambiguous.childMeaning: Open to more than one meaning.
practiceSentences: The headline was ambiguous, and probably on purpose.
Which word makes this sentence ambiguous?
An ambiguous statement lets a speaker deny either reading.
She rewrote the ambiguous clause into two plain ones.
Ambiguous offers two clear meanings; vague offers none.

analytical.childMeaning: Examining something by breaking it into its parts.
practiceSentences: An analytical approach found the fault in an afternoon.
What analytical skills does this job actually need?
Analytical work separates a problem before solving it.
Her analytical report was longer and far more useful.
Analytical takes apart; holistic looks at the whole.

anecdote.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept.
practiceSentences: Grandmother's anecdote about the flood explained the whole family.
What anecdote would you tell about your own street?
An anecdote is evidence of a kind, but only of one kind.
He opened the talk with an anecdote and had the room at once.
An anecdote is true and small; a fable is invented and large.

antecedent.childMeaning: The word that a later pronoun refers back to.
practiceSentences: In that sentence the antecedent of "they" is unclear.
Which noun is the antecedent here?
A pronoun with no clear antecedent stops a reader dead.
She rewrote the paragraph to fix a missing antecedent.
An antecedent usually comes before, which is what the word means.
antecedent.note: Quoted an example in BACKTICKS - the eighth and ninth of this restructure, in a third consecutive grade, both caught by the rule added at Grade 6.

applicability.childMeaning: How far something can be usefully applied to a situation.
practiceSentences: The rule's applicability to festivals was never tested.
What is the applicability of this finding beyond one city?
Applicability is the question a reader asks after believing you.
They doubted the applicability of the study to a rural district.
Applicability asks where an idea works, not whether it is true.

appraise.childMeaning: To judge the worth or quality of something carefully.
practiceSentences: The manager appraises each apprentice twice a year.
How would you appraise your own first draft?
To appraise is to judge against a standard, not against a mood.
She appraised the offer for a week before answering.
Appraise is to assess; apprise is to inform, and they are different words.

approximation.childMeaning: A value or description that is close to the truth but not exact.
practiceSentences: Two thousand visitors was an approximation, not a count.
How good an approximation does this estimate give?
An approximation is honest as long as it says so.
The organisers worked from an approximation and were nearly right.
An approximation is close on purpose; an error is close by accident.

arbitrary.childMeaning: Chosen without a reason or rule behind it.
practiceSentences: The size labels are almost arbitrary between brands.
Is that cut-off arbitrary or is there a reason?
An arbitrary rule is hard to argue with and easy to resent.
The deadline felt arbitrary until she saw the shipping schedule.
Arbitrary means without reason; random means without pattern.

archetype.childMeaning: A character or pattern that appears again and again in stories.
practiceSentences: The wise elder is an archetype found in every culture.
Which archetype does this character follow?
An archetype is a shape a story reaches for without being told to.
The journey home is an archetype older than writing.
Recognising an archetype is not the same as calling it a cliche.

aspiration.note: Sentence 5 was 'Talk about your own aspiration.' - a speaking-task instruction rather than a sentence teaching the word - and sentence 1 named Sami, who is not in this grade's readings.
practiceSentences: Jamal's aspiration to become a pilot began the day he first watched planes from the airport fence.
Does every aspiration need a deadline, or can some dreams stay open-ended?
"Write down one aspiration," said the careers adviser, "then list three steps that lead towards it."
My deepest aspiration is to open a school in my grandparents' village one day.
An aspiration without a first step stays a wish.

assonance.childMeaning: The repeating of vowel sounds in nearby words.
practiceSentences: The assonance in deep green sea slows the line down.
Where is the assonance in this stanza?
Assonance binds a line without the chime of a full rhyme.
Poets use assonance where rhyme would be too loud.
Assonance repeats vowels; alliteration repeats the opening sounds.

assumption.childMeaning: Something taken to be true without being checked.
practiceSentences: The whole plan rested on an assumption nobody had tested.
What assumption is this advertisement making about you?
An assumption is a decision you did not notice making.
She listed her assumptions before starting the calculation.
An assumption is unexamined; a premise is stated on purpose.

audit.childMeaning: An official check of records or practices.
practiceSentences: An independent audit found three suppliers the brand had not declared.
Who pays for the audit, and does that matter?
An audit checks what was done, not what was intended.
The factory passed its audit and failed the surprise visit.
An audit inspects the record; an inspection looks at the place.

autonomous.childMeaning: Able to act and decide independently.
practiceSentences: The team was autonomous within an agreed budget.
How autonomous should a first-year apprentice be?
Autonomous means answerable for the decision as well as free to make it.
She wanted an autonomous role and got a lonely one.
Autonomous governs itself; independent is simply not governed by another.

auxiliary.childMeaning: A helping verb used with a main verb.
practiceSentences: In "she has finished", the auxiliary is "has".
Which auxiliary would make this a question?
An auxiliary carries the tense so the main verb need not.
English builds most of its tenses out of auxiliaries.
An auxiliary helps; the main verb does the meaning.
auxiliary.note: Quoted an example in BACKTICKS - the eighth and ninth of this restructure, in a third consecutive grade, both caught by the rule added at Grade 6.

avatar.childMeaning: An image or figure standing for a person online.
practiceSentences: Her avatar is a drawing of a heron.
What does your choice of avatar tell a stranger?
An avatar hides a face and reveals a preference.
The forum required an avatar and a name that was not your own.
An avatar represents you; it is not a portrait of you.

ballad.childMeaning: A poem or song that tells a story, often handed down.
practiceSentences: The ballad carried the family's history for four generations.
How old is this ballad thought to be?
A ballad tells a story in verses and usually a refrain.
Jamal set the old ballad to a new tune.
A ballad survives because it is easy to remember.

bearing.childMeaning: A direction measured in degrees from north.
bearing.repitchedFrom: grade 8 unit 10: 'Carrying or supporting weight, responsibility, or meaning.' - a real sense of the word, and the wrong one on a card sitting between contour and geospatial. Here a bearing is what a walker takes off a compass.
practiceSentences: Take a bearing on the tower before the mist closes in.
What bearing would carry you back to the road?
A bearing is always measured clockwise from north.
She wrote the bearing down rather than trusting her memory.
Bearing also means carrying something, which is a different word doing double duty.

benchmark.childMeaning: A standard that other things are measured against.
practiceSentences: The industry benchmark for water use is rarely met.
Against what benchmark are you judging this?
A benchmark is only useful if somebody actually reaches it.
They set a benchmark and published it, which was the brave part.
A benchmark is a reference point, not a target.

biased.childMeaning: Unfairly favouring one side over another.
practiceSentences: The report was biased in what it left out, not in what it said.
Is this source biased, and does it declare it?
A biased account can contain nothing but true statements.
She read two biased papers to find the shape of the argument.
Biased leans one way; balanced gives each side its best case.

biometric.childMeaning: Using a physical feature, such as a fingerprint, to identify someone.
practiceSentences: Biometric locks read a fingerprint instead of a key.
What happens if biometric data is stolen?
A biometric cannot be changed once it has leaked.
The border post introduced biometric checks last year.
A password can be replaced; a biometric cannot.

biotic.childMeaning: To do with the living parts of an environment.
practiceSentences: Predators and competitors are biotic factors.
What biotic pressures act on this population?
A biotic factor is another organism affecting yours.
Biotic and abiotic factors together decide who survives.
Biotic covers everything alive, including what is too small to see.
A scatter graph is bivariate by definition.
What bivariate relationship is this study testing?
Bivariate data pairs each measurement with another.
She plotted the bivariate data and the pattern appeared.
Bivariate is two variables; univariate is one.

blockchain.childMeaning: A shared record of transactions that is very hard to alter.
practiceSentences: A blockchain stores each record in a chain that would have to be rewritten whole.
What problem is a blockchain actually solving here?
A blockchain removes the need to trust one central keeper.
The land registry trialled a blockchain and kept the paper copies.
A blockchain makes a record hard to change; it does not make it true.

bureaucracy.note: Sentences 1 and 2 were the same sentence - 'The new bureaucracy buried every simple request under a mountain of stamps, forms and signatures.' beside 'The endless bureaucracy of stamps and forms delayed even the simplest requests.' Same idea, same stamps, same forms.
practiceSentences: The bureaucracy buried every simple request under stamps and signatures.
Why does so much bureaucracy make helping ordinary people feel almost impossible?
A bureaucracy exists to apply a rule the same way to everyone, which is its virtue and its fault.
"This bureaucracy is designed to exhaust us," the elder muttered wearily.
I grew frustrated with the bureaucracy that turned one letter into weeks of waiting.

cadence.childMeaning: The rhythm and rise and fall of a voice or a line.
practiceSentences: The speaker's cadence carried the crowd more than the words did.
How would you describe the cadence of this passage?
Cadence is what survives when a poem is translated badly.
The drummer matched the cadence of the chant exactly.
Cadence is the music of speech, whether or not it is sung.

caesura.childMeaning: A pause inside a line of poetry.
practiceSentences: The caesura in the middle of the line forces a breath.
Where does the caesura fall in this verse?
A caesura breaks a line without ending it.
The poet uses a caesura to make the reader stop and reconsider.
A caesura pauses within a line; a line break ends one.

capitalism.note: Three of the five sentences said the same thing: 'In a country built on capitalism, many small businesses compete to win the trust of shoppers.', 'Under capitalism, individuals can open businesses and compete freely to sell their goods.' and 'Under capitalism, shopkeepers compete for customers by offering better prices and fresher goods each week.' One idea, three times, on one card.
practiceSentences: Under capitalism, businesses are privately owned and compete for customers.
What are the main strengths and weaknesses of capitalism as an economic system?
Capitalism rewards what sells, which is not always what lasts.
Fast fashion is capitalism working exactly as designed, at speed.
I researched how capitalism shapes the prices we pay in ordinary shops.

caricature.childMeaning: A picture or description that exaggerates features for effect.
practiceSentences: The caricature gave the minister an enormous chin.
Which feature does this caricature exaggerate?
A caricature works because it is recognisable and unfair.
The article was a caricature of a complicated argument.
A caricature exaggerates what is there; a fabrication invents it.

cellular.childMeaning: To do with the cells that living things are made of.
practiceSentences: Recovery happens at a cellular level long before it is felt.
What cellular change does endurance training cause?
Cellular damage from hard effort is repaired during sleep.
The study measured cellular oxygen use during a sprint.
Cellular also describes a phone network built from cells.

civic-minded.childMeaning: Caring about the good of your town or community.
practiceSentences: A civic-minded neighbour reports the broken light nobody else mentions.
What makes a person civic-minded?
Civic-minded is public spirit turned into small habits.
Kofi is civic-minded enough to attend the meetings nobody enjoys.
Civic-minded is about the community; ambitious is about yourself.

coding-based.childMeaning: Built on written program instructions rather than on ready-made tools.
practiceSentences: The club runs a coding-based course rather than a drag-and-drop one.
Is a coding-based approach harder to start and easier to extend?
A coding-based solution can be changed by anyone who reads it.
They chose a coding-based tool so the school could adapt it.
Coding-based means somebody wrote the instructions rather than clicked them.

colonialism.childMeaning: One country taking control of another and settling or ruling it.
practiceSentences: Colonialism redrew the borders this region still uses.
How long did colonialism last in this part of the coast?
Colonialism changed languages as thoroughly as it changed maps.
The museum's new wing examines colonialism honestly.
Colonialism ended as a system long before its effects did.

compelling.childMeaning: So convincing or interesting that it holds your attention.
practiceSentences: The evidence for the new method is compelling.
What makes this argument compelling rather than merely loud?
A compelling case anticipates the strongest objection.
Her compelling final lap changed how the race is remembered.
Compelling persuades; forceful only pushes.

complexity.childMeaning: The state of having many parts that affect one another.
practiceSentences: The complexity of a supply chain hides where the harm happens.
How much complexity can one label usefully carry?
Complexity is not the same as difficulty.
The complexity of the dye process surprised the whole class.
Complexity is why simple answers about clothing are usually wrong.

composition.childMeaning: What something is made of, or the way its parts are arranged.
practiceSentences: The label lists the composition of the fabric.
What is the composition of this blend?
Composition decides how a garment wears and how it washes.
The composition of the class photograph took twenty minutes.
Composition can mean the mixture, or the arrangement, or a piece of writing.

compression.childMeaning: Making a file smaller so it takes less space to store or send.
practiceSentences: Compression cut the video to a third of its size.
What does this compression throw away?
Lossless compression keeps everything; lossy compression does not.
Heavy compression turned the photograph into visible squares.
Compression saves space and sometimes spends quality.

concise.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept.
practiceSentences: A concise covering letter is read; a long one is skimmed.
Can you make this concise without losing the argument?
Concise writing takes longer to produce than loose writing.
She rewrote the summary three times to make it concise.
Concise says it in few words; brief only means short.

concurrent.childMeaning: Happening at the same time as something else.
practiceSentences: Three concurrent performances made choosing difficult.
Were the two ceremonies concurrent or one after the other?
Concurrent events split an audience.
The concurrent rehearsals used opposite ends of the hall.
Concurrent means alongside in time; consecutive means one then the next.

conditional.note: Sentence 3 named Teacher Yasmin, who belongs to Grade 5 - and the set held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: A conditional clause tells the reader exactly what must happen first.
Did you notice the conditional sentence hidden in the second paragraph?
"Every conditional sentence needs two matching halves," the teacher explained.
I realised that a conditional sentence can change the whole meaning of a promise.
A conditional makes a claim depend on something else being true.

consistency.childMeaning: Behaving or happening in the same way each time.
practiceSentences: The dye lacked consistency between batches.
Is there consistency between what the brand says and what it does?
Consistency is what makes a claim testable.
Her consistency over eight months persuaded the buyer.
Consistency also describes how thick or thin a liquid is.

construction.childMeaning: The building of something, or the way it is put together.
practiceSentences: Construction of the ring road took four years.
What construction method suits soft ground?
Construction is the noisiest promise a city ever makes.
The bridge's construction used far less steel than expected.
Construction can mean the building, the process, or the arrangement of a sentence.

contextual.childMeaning: Depending on the surrounding situation for its meaning.
practiceSentences: The reading is contextual: the same figure means different things in wet and dry seasons.
What contextual information does this graph leave out?
A contextual judgement cannot be transferred whole to another site.
She added contextual notes so the numbers could be read later.
Contextual means it depends on the setting; absolute means it does not.

contour.childMeaning: A line on a map joining points of equal height.
practiceSentences: Contour lines close together mean a steep slope.
What height does this contour represent?
Contours turn a flat map into a landscape you can read.
The path follows a single contour around the hill.
A contour joins equal heights; a gradient measures the change between them.

convection.childMeaning: The movement of heat by a flowing liquid or gas.
practiceSentences: Convection carries warm air up the valley each afternoon.
How does convection form a cloud?
Convection needs something that can flow.
The kettle heats by convection long before the water boils.
Convection moves the heat with the fluid; conduction passes it through a solid.

cooperative.childMeaning: Working willingly with others, or a business owned by its members.
practiceSentences: The festival is run by a cooperative of twelve families.
Was the response cooperative or merely polite?
A cooperative shares its profits among the people who made them.
Their cooperative approach finished the work in half the time.
Cooperative describes an attitude, and also a kind of company.

coordinating.childMeaning: Describing a word that joins two parts of equal weight.
practiceSentences: And, but and or are coordinating conjunctions.
Which coordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A coordinating conjunction joins equals; neither clause depends on the other.
She used a coordinating conjunction where a full stop would have been stronger.
Coordinating joins equals; subordinating makes one depend on the other.

copular.childMeaning: Describing a verb that links a subject to what is said about it.
practiceSentences: In she is a dancer, is is a copular verb.
Which copular verb would you use here?
A copular verb joins rather than acts.
Be, seem and become are the commonest copular verbs.
A copular verb takes no object; it takes a complement.

correlate.childMeaning: To show that two things change together.
practiceSentences: The two sets of readings correlate closely.
Does reading time correlate with the results here?
Two things can correlate without either causing the other.
She correlated the rainfall with the harvest over ten years.
To correlate is to move together; to cause is another claim entirely.

correlation.childMeaning: A relationship in which two things change together.
practiceSentences: There is a correlation between training hours and finishing times.
What correlation does this graph show?
Correlation is not causation, which is the most repeated warning in statistics.
A strong correlation can still be a coincidence.
A correlation can be positive, negative, or absent.

correlative.childMeaning: Describing a pair of words that work together in a sentence.
practiceSentences: Either and or are correlative conjunctions.
Which correlative pair would suit this sentence?
A correlative pair must match: neither goes with nor.
She used the correlative pair not only and but also in one sentence.
Correlative conjunctions come in pairs; coordinating ones stand alone.
correlative.note: Sentence 4 named the pair without using the word the card teaches.

couplet.childMeaning: Two lines of poetry that go together, usually rhyming.
practiceSentences: The poem closes on a couplet that answers its own question.
Which couplet carries the turn in this sonnet?
A couplet is short enough to remember and quote.
She ended each stanza with a rhyming couplet.
A couplet is two lines; a stanza may be many.

creativity.note: Sentences 1 and 4 named Milo and Tia, neither of whom is in this grade's readings, and all five were about a comic strip and a writing club - which is unit 3's world, not a unit about cities and transport.
practiceSentences: The bus shelter design showed real creativity within a tiny budget.
What sparks your creativity most, a strange image or an unusual sound?
Creativity in planning is usually a constraint met well.
Zara's proposal proved that creativity can come from the smallest, quietest ideas.
Certainly, the energy and creativity of young East Africans are making a difference.

credibility.childMeaning: The quality of deserving to be believed.
practiceSentences: The council lost credibility when the third deadline passed.
What gives this report its credibility?
Credibility is slow to build and quick to spend.
Publishing the raw figures restored some credibility.
Credibility is about the source; plausibility is about the claim.

cumulative.childMeaning: Growing by steady addition over time.
practiceSentences: The cumulative effect of small donations paid for the stage.
What is the cumulative total after four days?
A cumulative change is invisible until you look back.
Her cumulative experience of eight festivals showed in the planning.
Cumulative adds up; average smooths out.

cyberattack.childMeaning: A deliberate attempt to damage or break into a computer system.
practiceSentences: The cyberattack shut the booking system for two days.
How would a school notice a cyberattack early?
A cyberattack often begins with one convincing email.
The hospital's cyberattack delayed operations, not just paperwork.
A cyberattack is the event; cybercrime is the offence.

cybercrime.childMeaning: Criminal activity carried out using computers or networks.
practiceSentences: Cybercrime now costs more than many kinds of theft.
What makes cybercrime difficult to prosecute?
Cybercrime crosses borders faster than the law follows.
The unit investigates cybercrime reported by small businesses.
Cybercrime is the category; a cyberattack is one act within it.

data-driven.childMeaning: Decided by what the measurements show rather than by opinion.
practiceSentences: The timetable change was data-driven and unpopular.
What makes a decision data-driven rather than data-decorated?
A data-driven decision is only as good as the data behind it.
Their data-driven approach found a problem nobody had reported.
Data-driven follows the evidence; evidence-led admits judgement is still involved.

deconstruct.childMeaning: To take an argument or text apart to see how it works.
practiceSentences: Deconstruct the advertisement before you judge it.
How would you deconstruct this opening paragraph?
To deconstruct is to expose the assumptions holding a thing up.
She deconstructed the speech line by line.
To deconstruct is to take apart; to destroy is not the same word.

decryption.childMeaning: Turning coded information back into a readable form.
practiceSentences: Decryption needs the key, not merely the method.
How long would decryption take without the key?
Decryption is encryption run backwards, and only with permission.
The archive released the decryption key after fifty years.
Encryption locks the message; decryption opens it.

defend.note: All five inherited sentences were about fake news, rumours and reliable sources - which is unit 8's subject - and one named Rohan, who is not in this grade's readings. Here the word sits among appraise, weigh and reassess, where defending is what you do with a claim you have made.
practiceSentences: Be ready to defend every figure in the proposal.
How would you defend this decision to somebody who disagrees?
To defend a claim is to give the reasons, not to repeat it louder.
Imani defended her conclusion without once raising her voice.
A claim you cannot defend is a claim you should not have made.
The pause before the drums was deliberate.
Was the omission deliberate or an oversight?
A deliberate choice can still be the wrong one.
She made a deliberate decision to keep the ceremony short.
Deliberate as an adjective means intended; as a verb it means to think it over.

delineate.childMeaning: To describe or mark out something precisely.
practiceSentences: The report delineates each stage of the supply chain.
Can you delineate where the responsibility ends?
To delineate is to draw the line, not to argue about it.
She delineated three problems and solved the smallest.
Delineate means to outline exactly; to outline can mean roughly.

demographic.childMeaning: To do with the make-up of a population, such as age or income.
practiceSentences: The demographic change was clear in the school rolls.
Which demographic uses this bus route most?
A demographic is a group described by a measurement, not by choice.
Demographic data decided where the new clinic went.
Demographic describes a population; democratic describes how it votes.

determiner.childMeaning: A word before a noun that shows which one or how many.
practiceSentences: The, this and every are determiners.
Which determiner makes the meaning most specific?
A determiner narrows a noun before any adjective does.
English requires a determiner where many languages do not.
A determiner points; an adjective describes.

diagnose.childMeaning: To identify what is wrong from the signs available.
practiceSentences: The ranger diagnosed the die-off as a water problem.
How would you diagnose the cause of this decline?
To diagnose is to name a cause, not just a symptom.
She diagnosed the fault in the pump within minutes.
Diagnosing comes before treating, and is the harder half.

differentiation.childMeaning: The act of telling or making things different from one another.
practiceSentences: Differentiation between the two routes matters at rush hour.
What differentiation does this map actually show?
Differentiation begins with noticing that a difference exists.
The survey used colour for differentiation between districts.
Differentiation also names a method in mathematics.

digitalisation.childMeaning: Changing how an organisation works by moving it onto digital systems.
practiceSentences: Digitalisation turned three filing rooms into one server.
What has digitalisation cost the people who ran those rooms?
Digitalisation changes the work, not only the storage.
The hospital's digitalisation took four years and two false starts.
Digitising converts a document; digitalisation changes the whole process.

dioxide.childMeaning: A compound containing two oxygen atoms joined to another element.
dioxide.repitchedFrom: grade 2 unit 7: 'Dioxide is part of the name of a gas that plants breathe in.' It restated its own headword, was pitched five grades below this one, and was not quite right besides - dioxide names two oxygen atoms, not a gas. It arrived on a card sitting beside reactant, convection and equilibrium.
practiceSentences: Carbon dioxide holds one carbon atom and two of oxygen.
Which dioxide is produced when sulphur burns?
The di in dioxide means two, as it does in dialogue.
Sulphur dioxide from the works turned the rain acidic.
A dioxide has two oxygens; a monoxide has one.

discern.childMeaning: To notice or understand something that is not obvious.
discern.note: The inherited meaning began lowercase and ended without a full stop - the shape that has appeared in every grade of this restructure so far.
practiceSentences: It is hard to discern the writer's real view from one page.
What can you discern from the handwriting alone?
To discern is to see a difference others miss.
She discerned a pattern in the dates that nobody had noticed.
To discern is to perceive carefully; to judge is what comes next.

discovery.childMeaning: The finding of something that was not known before.
practiceSentences: The discovery of the nesting site changed the whole survey.
What discovery would settle this question?
A discovery is only the beginning of the work.
Her discovery was published two years after she made it.
A discovery finds what existed; an invention makes what did not.

distillation.childMeaning: Separating liquids by boiling them and cooling the vapour.
practiceSentences: Distillation recovers the solvent so it can be used again.
How does distillation separate two liquids?
Distillation works because different liquids boil at different temperatures.
The recovered solvent came back from distillation almost pure.
Distillation separates by boiling point; filtration separates by size.

distinct.childMeaning: Clearly separate and different from others.
practiceSentences: Each region brings a distinct dish to the festival.
Are these two traditions distinct or simply differently named?
A distinct difference is one you can point to.
The drumming of the two villages is quite distinct.
Distinct means clearly separate; distinctive means clearly recognisable.

dominant.childMeaning: Most powerful or most common in a situation.
practiceSentences: Cotton remains the dominant fibre in the trade.
Which brand is dominant in this market?
A dominant supplier sets terms the others accept.
The dominant colour of the season changes every year on purpose.
Dominant means it prevails, not that it deserves to.

ecology-based.childMeaning: Founded on how living things relate to each other and their surroundings.
practiceSentences: An ecology-based design works with the slope instead of against it.
What would an ecology-based farm look like here?
Ecology-based thinking asks what else a change will touch.
The scheme is ecology-based and deliberately unhurried.
Ecology-based starts from relationships; engineering starts from structures.

ecosystem-based.childMeaning: Working with a whole habitat rather than one species at a time.
practiceSentences: An ecosystem-based plan protects the river as well as the fish.
Why is an ecosystem-based approach slower to show results?
Ecosystem-based management treats the system as the unit.
The reserve adopted an ecosystem-based policy after the first plan failed.
Ecosystem-based means the whole habitat is the thing being managed.

effectiveness.childMeaning: How well something achieves what it was meant to.
practiceSentences: The effectiveness of the fence was measured over three seasons.
How would you test the effectiveness of this method?
Effectiveness asks whether it worked, not whether it was cheap.
The scheme's effectiveness fell once the funding ended.
Effectiveness is doing the right thing; efficiency is doing it with less.

electorate.childMeaning: All the people entitled to vote in an election.
practiceSentences: The electorate grew by forty thousand this year.
What does the electorate actually want here?
An electorate is a group defined by a right, not by an opinion.
Newspapers claim to speak for an electorate that never asked them to.
The electorate votes; the government governs.

electromagnetic.childMeaning: To do with the waves that carry light, radio and X-rays.
practiceSentences: Radio and visible light are both electromagnetic waves.
Which electromagnetic waves does this device use?
Electromagnetic waves need no material to travel through.
The whole wireless network runs on electromagnetic radiation.
The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves to gamma rays.

elegy.childMeaning: A poem written in mourning for someone who has died.
practiceSentences: The elegy was read at the close of the festival.
For whom was this elegy written?
An elegy grieves, and often ends by consoling.
Amara wrote an elegy for the tree the storm took.
An elegy mourns; a eulogy praises at the funeral itself.

ellipsis.childMeaning: Leaving out words that the reader can supply from context.
practiceSentences: In she can code and he cannot, ellipsis removes the second code.
Where has ellipsis been used in this sentence?
Ellipsis avoids repeating what has just been said.
Speech uses ellipsis constantly without anyone noticing.
Ellipsis also names the three dots that mark an omission.

emission.childMeaning: Something released into the air or water, especially waste gas.
practiceSentences: Textile production accounts for a large share of global emissions.
What emission does this stage of the process produce?
An emission is invisible and still measurable.
The factory cut its emissions by changing one solvent.
Emission is the releasing, and also the thing released.

empirical.childMeaning: Based on what has been observed or measured.
practiceSentences: The claim is empirical, so it can be checked.
What empirical evidence supports this?
An empirical answer beats a confident one.
Their empirical work took six seasons of counting.
Empirical rests on observation; theoretical rests on reasoning.

endocrine.childMeaning: To do with the glands that release hormones into the blood.
practiceSentences: The endocrine system controls growth and recovery.
Which endocrine gland releases adrenaline?
The endocrine system works slowly, through the bloodstream.
Endocrine signals reach every cell rather than one target.
The endocrine system uses chemicals; the nervous system uses electricity.

enjambment.childMeaning: When a sentence runs on past the end of a line without a pause.
practiceSentences: Enjambment carries the sense over the line break.
Why does the poet use enjambment here?
Enjambment makes a poem sound closer to speech.
The enjambment leaves the reader briefly unsure how the line ends.
Enjambment runs over; a stopped line rests at its end.

entrepreneur.note: Inherited whole and kept - varied, inside the cap, and about starting a business, which is this unit's subject.
practiceSentences: The young entrepreneur turned her grandmother's recipes into a thriving catering business.
What qualities must an entrepreneur possess to survive the risky first year of a new business?
"Every entrepreneur fails at something first," the speaker admitted, "and those failures become the best lessons."
I dream of becoming an entrepreneur who builds affordable solar lamps for villages without electricity.
Today he is a successful entrepreneur who employs three other young people.

enumerate.childMeaning: To name things one by one in order.
practiceSentences: Enumerate the reasons before you rank them.
Can you enumerate the steps in the argument?
To enumerate is to list with a number attached.
She enumerated four objections and answered three.
Enumerate names each one; summarise gathers them together.

epigram.childMeaning: A short, sharp saying that makes its point wittily.
practiceSentences: The essay closes on an epigram nobody forgets.
Which epigram would you choose for the title page?
An epigram must be short enough to repeat from memory.
She wrote an epigram where a paragraph had been.
An epigram is witty and brief; a proverb is old and anonymous.

epilogue.childMeaning: A closing section that comes after the main story ends.
practiceSentences: The epilogue tells us what became of each of them.
What does the epilogue add that the ending did not?
An epilogue answers the question a reader is left holding.
The epilogue jumps forward twenty years in a page.
An epilogue is not a second ending; it is the view from later.

equilibrium.childMeaning: A state of balance where opposing forces cancel out.
practiceSentences: The population reached an equilibrium after four seasons.
What would upset the equilibrium of this pool?
An equilibrium is not stillness; it is change that balances.
Removing one predator ended the equilibrium within a year.
An equilibrium can be stable or precarious, and looks identical until it is tested.

equity.childMeaning: Fairness that takes account of different needs.
practiceSentences: Equity gives each district what it needs, not the same amount.
Is equity fairer than equality here?
Equity treats people differently in order to treat them fairly.
The transport plan aimed at equity between the old city and the new.
Equity also means the value you own in a house or a business.

euphemism.childMeaning: A mild word used in place of a blunt or unpleasant one.
practiceSentences: Letting staff go is a euphemism for dismissing them.
Which euphemism is this report hiding behind?
A euphemism softens the sentence and hides the fact.
She replaced every euphemism with the plain word and the piece changed entirely.
A euphemism is polite; a lie is not, but the distance can be short.

exclamatory.childMeaning: Describing a sentence that expresses strong feeling.
practiceSentences: What a difference a year makes is an exclamatory sentence.
Which exclamatory sentence would suit this ending?
An exclamatory sentence ends with an exclamation mark.
She cut every exclamatory sentence from the formal letter.
An exclamatory sentence exclaims; a declarative one states.

exponential.childMeaning: Growing by a multiplying factor each step, so it accelerates.
practiceSentences: Exponential growth looks slow until it suddenly does not.
Is this growth exponential or merely fast?
An exponential curve doubles in a fixed time, again and again.
The number of connected devices grew exponentially for a decade.
Exponential multiplies each step; linear only adds.

fable.childMeaning: A short invented story that carries a lesson, often with animals.
practiceSentences: The fable ends with the moral stated outright.
What lesson does this fable actually teach?
A fable uses animals so nobody has to be blamed.
She wrote a fable about a river that stopped listening.
A fable admits it is invented; an anecdote does not.

facilitate.note: Inherited whole from grade 8 and kept - varied, inside the cap, and about a footbridge and a residents' meeting, which is this unit's world.
practiceSentences: Clear instructions facilitate teamwork when dozens of helpers arrive at once.
The new footbridge will facilitate safe school journeys for children from both sides of the river.
Could a shared calendar facilitate cooperation between the museum, the library and the sports club?
"My role is to facilitate, not decide," explained the chairperson, opening the residents' meeting.
I volunteered to facilitate the younger pupils' discussion group, and their ideas honestly amazed me.

finite.childMeaning: Describing a verb form that shows tense and agrees with its subject.
practiceSentences: In she walks home, walks is the finite verb.
Which verb in this clause is finite?
Every complete sentence needs at least one finite verb.
A finite verb changes with the subject; an infinitive does not.
Finite here means limited by tense and person, not merely countable.

flawed.note: Meaning inherited from grade 6 and kept.
practiceSentences: The survey was flawed because only readers replied.
What makes this method flawed rather than merely limited?
A flawed study can still point in the right direction.
The argument is flawed at its second step.
Flawed means it has a fault; false means it is wrong.

flexibility.childMeaning: The ability to change easily to suit new conditions.
practiceSentences: A plan needs flexibility when the weather decides the timetable.
What flexibility does this route allow?
Flexibility costs something: a flexible plan is rarely the cheapest.
The team's flexibility saved the expedition on day four.
Flexibility bends; fragility breaks.

forecast.childMeaning: To say what is likely to happen, using what is known now.
practiceSentences: They forecast the rains three weeks early and were right.
What does the model forecast for the next decade?
To forecast is to be precise about uncertainty.
The forecast was wrong, which is not the same as careless.
A forecast states a probability; a prediction often pretends not to.

frame.childMeaning: To present an idea in a way that shapes how it is understood.
frame.repitchedFrom: grade 3 unit 5: 'A strong structure that holds something up or gives it shape.' - the physical sense, four grades below this card, which sits between rank and weigh among the reasoning verbs. Here to frame a question is to decide what it is about. The physical sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: How you frame the question decides which answers are possible.
Would you frame this as a cost or as an investment?
To frame an argument is to choose what it is about before arguing it.
She framed the delay as a chance to test the design again.
Frame also means the structure that holds something up.

generalisation.childMeaning: A broad conclusion drawn from particular cases.
practiceSentences: One dry season is not enough for a generalisation.
What generalisation does this data actually support?
A generalisation is useful until it meets the case it cannot hold.
She avoided a generalisation and reported what she saw.
A generalisation reaches beyond the evidence, which is its purpose and its risk.

genetics.childMeaning: The study of how features are passed from parents to offspring.
practiceSentences: Genetics explains part of an athlete's ceiling, not all of it.
What does genetics contribute to endurance?
Genetics loads the dice; training rolls them.
She studied genetics after a season of injuries.
Genetics is the study; genes are what it studies.

geolocation.childMeaning: Working out where a device or person is on the Earth.
practiceSentences: Geolocation put the photograph within ten metres of the harbour.
What geolocation data does this app send?
Geolocation is useful, and it is also a record of where you have been.
She turned geolocation off before posting the picture.
Geolocation finds a position; a map only shows one.

geospatial.childMeaning: To do with data tied to a position on the Earth.
practiceSentences: Geospatial data showed where the flooding would reach first.
What geospatial information does this app collect?
Geospatial means every record carries a location.
The council used geospatial analysis to place the bus stops.
Geospatial data is ordinary data with a where attached.

gerund.childMeaning: An -ing form of a verb used as a noun.
practiceSentences: In walking is cheap, walking is a gerund.
Which gerund is the subject here?
A gerund looks like a verb and behaves like a noun.
She listed swimming, climbing and reading as gerunds.
A gerund names the activity; a participle describes something.

globalisation.childMeaning: The growing connection of the world's economies and cultures.
practiceSentences: Globalisation put the same shop signs in four continents.
What has globalisation cost this town?
Globalisation moves goods faster than it moves the people who make them.
The port's expansion was globalisation arriving in one building.
Globalisation connects markets; internationalism cooperates between states.

governance.childMeaning: The way an organisation or country is run and held to account.
practiceSentences: Good governance shows up in the drains before it shows up in speeches.
Who is responsible for the governance of this scheme?
Governance is not the same as government: a club has governance too.
Weak governance let three contracts go unexamined.
Governance is how decisions get made and who answers for them.

greenhouse.childMeaning: Describing gases that trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere.
practiceSentences: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
How does the greenhouse effect keep the planet liveable?
The greenhouse effect is natural; its strengthening is not.
Greenhouse gases let sunlight in and slow the heat leaving.
A greenhouse is also a glass building, which is where the comparison comes from.

holistic.childMeaning: Considering something as a whole rather than in parts.
practiceSentences: A holistic survey records the soil as well as the birds.
What would a holistic view of this valley include?
A holistic approach resists solving one problem into another.
The report took a holistic view and was twice as long.
Holistic looks at the whole; reductive takes it apart.

hypothetical.childMeaning: Imagined for the sake of argument rather than real.
practiceSentences: Take a hypothetical class of thirty and work it through.
Is that a hypothetical case or one that happened?
A hypothetical example tests an argument without accusing anyone.
She answered the hypothetical question and refused the real one.
Hypothetical is supposed for argument; theoretical rests on a theory.

ideology.childMeaning: A connected set of beliefs about how society should work.
practiceSentences: Every ideology explains what is wrong and who should fix it.
Which ideology does this pamphlet argue for?
An ideology answers questions before they are asked.
She traced the ideology back to two nineteenth-century books.
An ideology is a system of belief, not simply an opinion.

immunity.childMeaning: The body's ability to resist a particular disease.
practiceSentences: Immunity can come from having the illness or from a vaccine.
How long does immunity to this virus last?
Immunity is specific: it protects against one thing, not everything.
Hard training can lower immunity for a day or two.
Immunity also means being protected from a rule or a penalty.

imperative.note: Meaning inherited from grade 5 and kept - it is precise and needs no re-pitching.
practiceSentences: Run, jump and throw are all imperatives here.
Which imperative opens the coach's instructions?
An imperative gives an order and often drops its subject.
The signs used the imperative because there was no time to be polite.
An imperative commands; an interrogative asks.

implication.note: The inherited set held four sentences, not five. Kept otherwise - it is this unit's own subject and inside the cap.
practiceSentences: The implication of the new fitness data was that the squad needed longer recovery periods.
What is the implication for smaller schools if the league raises its entry fees again?
"The implication of your silence," said the captain quietly, "is that you disagree with the plan."
I resented the implication that our team had won only because the referee favoured us.
An implication is carried by a statement; an inference is drawn by a listener.

improvement.note: All four inherited sentences were about writing and a school newspaper - checking facts, handling sources, a pupil's prose - which is unit 8's subject, not a unit about sport and achievement. Two of them named Teacher Yasmin, who belongs to Grade 5, and Rohan, who is not in this grade's readings. The set also held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: Real improvement often comes from small, steady changes rather than one big leap.
Has there been any improvement in her sprint times this season?
The coach measured improvement in seconds, not in effort.
An improvement you cannot measure is a feeling about an improvement.
Improvement plateaus, and the plateau is where most athletes stop.

indicative.childMeaning: Describing the verb form used to state a fact.
practiceSentences: In she runs every morning, runs is indicative.
Which mood is indicative in this passage?
The indicative states; it does not command or wish.
Almost every sentence you read is in the indicative.
The indicative reports what is; the subjunctive what might be.

inequality.childMeaning: An unfair difference in what people have or can get.
inequality.repitchedFrom: grade 5 unit 7: 'A statement that two amounts are not equal.' - the MATHEMATICAL sense, and this grade inherited it word for word with all five of its sentences, about x being greater than five and graphing on a number line. It is the ONE word the supplied list repeats from Grades 1-6, and unlike Grade 6's protagonist and density it is a genuine second sense rather than a duplicate card: the maths meaning is correct and belongs to Grade 5. Here the word sits beside governance, statute and marginalisation, where it is the social sense. Both are named, one on each card.
practiceSentences: Inequality shows in how long a journey to work takes.
What inequality does this map make visible?
Inequality is a difference that somebody could have prevented.
The report measured inequality between districts of the same city.
In mathematics an inequality is something else entirely: a statement that two amounts differ.

inevitable.note: The inherited set held four sentences, not five. Kept otherwise - it is this unit's own subject.
practiceSentences: After months of missed training sessions, the team's relegation began to feel inevitable.
Was the champion's defeat inevitable once the injury started affecting her landing?
"Mistakes are inevitable," the coach reassured us, "but repeating them is a choice."
I used to think losing to the city schools was inevitable, until our new goalkeeper proved otherwise.
Calling something inevitable afterwards is easier than predicting it before.

infinitive.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept - it is plain and names its own example.
practiceSentences: The infinitive is the form you find in a dictionary.
Which infinitive follows this verb?
An infinitive does not change with the subject.
She split the infinitive deliberately and nobody minded.
An infinitive names the action; a finite verb places it in time.

inflation.childMeaning: A general rise in prices, so money buys less than before.
inflation.note: Sentences 1 and 2 were the same sentence - wages buying fewer groceries, and a loaf costing far more than last year. Same idea, same shopping basket. The grade 6 meaning was also loose: 'when prices for things go up, so you need more money to buy the same things'.
practiceSentences: When inflation rises sharply, families discover that their weekly wages buy far fewer groceries.
How does inflation make it harder for families to afford their weekly shopping?
After the drought destroyed the crops, inflation pushed the price of maize far beyond most wages.
Inflation punishes savers and quietly forgives borrowers.
I learned that rapid inflation can shrink the value of money almost overnight.

inherent.childMeaning: Existing in something as a natural and permanent part of it.
practiceSentences: There is an inherent bias in any account written by a winner.
Is that limitation inherent, or could it be designed out?
An inherent quality cannot be removed without changing the thing.
The risk is inherent in the method, not in the operator.
Inherent means built in; incidental means it happened to be there.

innovate.note: The inherited set held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: Small schools can innovate just as effectively as large, well-funded companies.
What stops a community from choosing to innovate when resources are scarce?
Kofi, you never stop trying to innovate, even with the simplest materials!
Great teams innovate by asking better questions, not by having more money.
To innovate is to put a new idea to work, not merely to have one.

innovation.childMeaning: A new method or idea put into practice.
innovation.repitchedFrom: the inherited meaning opened 'Innovation is the introduction of new ideas, methods or inventions' - restating its own headword, and listing three nouns where one does the work.
practiceSentences: The clap-skate was an innovation that rewrote the record books.
What innovation changed this sport most?
An innovation is an idea that has actually been used.
Their innovation was a training schedule, not a machine.
An invention is made; an innovation is adopted.
Recovery is integral to a training plan, not an extra.
Is the warm-up integral or optional?
An integral part cannot be removed without changing the whole.
Her role became integral to how the team defended.
Integral means built in; important only means it matters.

intelligence.childMeaning: A machine's ability to perform tasks that would need human thought.
intelligence.repitchedFrom: grade 5 unit 8: 'The ability to learn, understand and think carefully about things', with sentences about octopuses opening jars and a little sister winning at memory games. That is the human sense, two grades below this card, which sits beside metadata, open-source and avatar. Here the word is artificial intelligence. The human sense is named in the fifth sentence, and the news sense in the fourth.
practiceSentences: Artificial intelligence now writes the first draft of some news reports.
What tasks does this intelligence actually perform?
An intelligence that sounds confident is not thereby correct.
Intelligence also means information gathered about an opponent.
Human intelligence and machine intelligence are not the same thing.
intelligence.note: My own sentence 5 opened 'And it still means...' - a continuation that only makes sense after sentence 4, which is precisely the cannot-stand-alone fault this restructure keeps finding in inherited content. Caught by the check because it also failed to use the headword.

internationalism.childMeaning: The belief that countries should work together for shared ends.
practiceSentences: The games were founded on a hopeful internationalism.
What does internationalism ask a country to give up?
Internationalism assumes problems do not stop at borders.
The festival's internationalism shows in its programme.
Internationalism cooperates between nations; globalisation connects their markets.

interoperability.childMeaning: The ability of different systems to work together.
practiceSentences: Interoperability lets two hospitals read the same record.
Why is interoperability so often promised and so rarely delivered?
Interoperability needs an agreed standard more than it needs good code.
The lack of interoperability cost the project a year.
Interoperability is systems cooperating; compatibility is one fitting another.

interpretation.childMeaning: The particular way something is understood or explained.
practiceSentences: The referee's interpretation of the rule decided the match.
What interpretation would you offer of this result?
An interpretation is a reading, and other readings exist.
Two officials gave opposite interpretations of the same contact.
An interpretation explains the evidence; the evidence does not explain itself.

interquartile.childMeaning: Describing the range covering the middle half of the data.
practiceSentences: The interquartile range ignores the fastest and slowest quarters.
What is the interquartile range of these times?
The interquartile range is not disturbed by one freak result.
She compared the interquartile ranges rather than the extremes.
Interquartile means between the quarters, which is exactly what it measures.

interrogate.childMeaning: To question something closely and searchingly.
practiceSentences: Interrogate the source before you quote it.
How would you interrogate this claim?
To interrogate a statistic is to ask who counted, and how.
She interrogated the data and found the missing month.
To interrogate is to question hard; to interview is to let somebody speak.

interrogative.childMeaning: Describing the form used to ask a question.
practiceSentences: Who, what and which are interrogative words.
Which interrogative would open this question?
An interrogative sentence usually reverses subject and verb.
She rewrote the statement as an interrogative to soften it.
An interrogative asks; an imperative tells.

intersectionality.childMeaning: The idea that parts of a person's identity overlap and act together.
practiceSentences: Intersectionality asks how two disadvantages combine rather than add.
Why does intersectionality matter when a policy is written?
Intersectionality treats a person as whole rather than as a category.
The essay used intersectionality to explain a result that puzzled everyone.
Intersectionality is a lens, not a verdict.

intransitive.childMeaning: Describing a verb that takes no object.
practiceSentences: In the river rose, rose is intransitive.
Is arrive transitive or intransitive?
An intransitive verb is complete without an object.
You cannot make an intransitive verb passive.
Intransitive verbs act without acting on anything.

investigation.note: Meaning inherited from grade 5 and kept - it is precise and needs no re-pitching.
practiceSentences: The investigation took four months and changed one paragraph of the report.
What investigation would settle the question?
An investigation follows the evidence rather than the suspicion.
She opened an investigation into how the post was advertised.
An investigation looks for facts; an inquiry may look for blame.

juxtaposition.childMeaning: Placing two things side by side so the contrast shows.
practiceSentences: The juxtaposition of the wedding and the funeral is deliberate.
What does this juxtaposition make you notice?
Juxtaposition argues without saying anything.
The photograph's juxtaposition of new tower and old well says it all.
Juxtaposition places side by side; comparison discusses the difference.

learning.childMeaning: A method by which a computer improves from data rather than from instructions.
learning.repitchedFrom: grade 1 unit 10: 'Learning is finding out new things and getting better at them.' It restated its own headword and came from SIX grades below - the largest gap found in this restructure - onto a card beside metadata and open-source, where the word means machine learning. The ordinary sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: Machine learning finds patterns nobody wrote down.
What data was this learning system trained on?
A learning system repeats whatever bias its data contained.
The recommendations improved as the learning continued.
Learning also means what you do when you find out something new.

legitimate.childMeaning: Allowed by rules or law, or reasonable and justified.
practiceSentences: The company holds a legitimate licence for the work.
Is that a legitimate reason for refusing the request?
A legitimate complaint deserves an answer even when it is inconvenient.
Her legitimate expectation was set out in the contract.
Legitimate can mean lawful, or simply fair enough.

lexical.childMeaning: To do with the words of a language rather than its grammar.
practiceSentences: The lexical choice between slim and skinny carries the whole judgement.
What lexical field does this poem draw on?
A lexical change alters which words are used, not how they are arranged.
She studied the lexical differences between the two translations.
Lexical is about vocabulary; syntactic is about structure.

liberty.childMeaning: The freedom to act and think without unfair restriction.
practiceSentences: Liberty is easiest to define by what it lacks.
What liberty did the reform actually deliver?
Liberty for one person can limit liberty for another.
The speech placed liberty above order, deliberately.
Liberty is a right; freedom is often a feeling.

limitation.childMeaning: Something that restricts what can be done or known.
practiceSentences: Every method has a limitation, and honest work names it.
What is the main limitation of this study?
A limitation stated is a limitation half answered.
Her only limitation was the time she could give it.
A limitation restricts; a weakness undermines.

linear.childMeaning: Changing by the same amount each step, so it plots as a straight line.
practiceSentences: The cost is linear: each extra user adds the same amount.
Is this relationship linear across the whole range?
A linear graph is a straight line, whatever its slope.
She fitted a linear model and it held for four years.
Linear adds the same each time; exponential multiplies.

loss.childMeaning: The amount of material or energy wasted in a process.
loss.repitchedFrom: the inherited meaning was 'The state of no longer having something, especially something valuable or important' - the everyday sense, with sentences about a lost projector and a team's captain, and one naming Theo, who belongs to Grades 2 and 3. On a card sitting between yield and distillation, loss is what a process wastes. The everyday sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: Cutting a pattern badly increases the loss of fabric.
What loss does each stage of this process accept?
A loss of ten per cent at four stages is not a loss of ten per cent.
Heat loss makes the dryer the costliest machine in the building.
Loss also means no longer having something you valued.

lyric.childMeaning: A short poem expressing personal feeling, or the words of a song.
practiceSentences: The lyric holds one moment rather than telling a story.
Which lyric did the singer open the festival with?
A lyric speaks in the first person more often than not.
Kofi set his grandmother's lyric to a drum rhythm.
A lyric expresses; a ballad narrates.

marginal.childMeaning: Small, or only just enough to matter.
practiceSentences: The saving from the new machine was marginal.
Is the difference marginal or worth reporting?
A marginal gain repeated a thousand times stops being marginal.
The change made a marginal difference to the water used.
Marginal also means at the edge, which is where the word comes from.

marginalisation.childMeaning: Pushing a group to the edge of a society's attention.
practiceSentences: Marginalisation shows in which streets get repaired.
What causes the marginalisation of a whole district?
Marginalisation is rarely announced; it is done by omission.
The report documented the marginalisation of families without cars.
Marginalisation is being left out of decisions, not only out of money.

metabolism.childMeaning: All the chemical processes that keep a living thing going.
practiceSentences: Training slowly changes an athlete's metabolism.
How does metabolism differ between rest and effort?
Metabolism is what turns food into movement and heat.
Her metabolism recovered faster than the coach expected.
Metabolism builds up and breaks down at the same time.

metadata.childMeaning: Information describing other information, such as when a file was made.
practiceSentences: The photograph's metadata gave the date and the place.
What metadata does this document carry?
Metadata often reveals more than the file it describes.
Journalists checked the metadata before believing the image.
Metadata is data about data, which is why it is easy to forget.

microbiology.childMeaning: The study of living things too small to see without a microscope.
practiceSentences: Microbiology explains why the water had to be boiled.
What can microbiology tell us that a symptom cannot?
Microbiology became possible only once lenses were good enough.
Her work in microbiology traced the outbreak to one well.
Microbiology studies the organisms; medicine treats what they do.

misinformation.childMeaning: False information spread without the spreader knowing it is wrong.
misinformation.repitchedFrom: the inherited meaning opened 'Misinformation is false or inaccurate information that is spread...' - restating its own headword. The set also held ONE sentence, which was about giving people space to explain rather than about the word.
practiceSentences: Misinformation spreads faster than the correction that follows it.
How would you check a story before passing the misinformation on?
Misinformation is not a lie: the person sharing it believes it.
One screenshot without a date started weeks of misinformation.
Misinformation is spread in error; disinformation is spread on purpose.

modifier.childMeaning: A word or phrase that changes the meaning of another word.
practiceSentences: A modifier placed wrongly can attach itself to the nearest noun.
Which modifier is doing the work in this phrase?
A modifier adds detail; it does not add a new idea.
Adjectives and adverbs are the commonest modifiers.
A dangling modifier describes something the sentence never mentions.

modify.childMeaning: To change something slightly to make it better or more suitable.
modify.note: The inherited meaning began lowercase and ended without a full stop - the shape that has now appeared in every grade of this restructure.
practiceSentences: They modified the junction rather than rebuilding it.
How would you modify this design for a narrower street?
To modify is to adjust what exists, not to replace it.
The plan was modified three times before approval.
In grammar, a word that modifies another changes its meaning.

monopoly.childMeaning: Control of a whole market by a single seller.
practiceSentences: A monopoly can set its price without looking at a rival.
How does a monopoly form in the first place?
A monopoly removes the pressure that keeps quality up.
Two firms supply almost the whole market, which is close to a monopoly.
A monopoly has one seller; a monopsony has one buyer.

morality.childMeaning: Beliefs about what is right and wrong behaviour.
practiceSentences: The debate turned on morality rather than on law.
Whose morality should a company follow?
Morality asks what ought to be done; law says what must be.
Her morality was formed long before the job tested it.
Morality is the system of belief; ethics is the study of it.

multiculturalism.childMeaning: The presence of many cultures within one society, valued together.
practiceSentences: The festival is multiculturalism made visible for a weekend.
What does multiculturalism ask of a city's schools?
Multiculturalism is a description of a place and also a policy towards it.
Three languages on one street sign is multiculturalism in practice.
Multiculturalism is more than several cultures in the same postcode.

mutation.childMeaning: A change in the genetic instructions of a living thing.
practiceSentences: A mutation can be harmful, helpful, or make no difference at all.
How often does a mutation occur naturally?
Most mutations do nothing an athlete would ever notice.
A single mutation explains this rare advantage in altitude.
Mutation supplies the variation that selection then acts on.

networked.childMeaning: Connected to other computers so information can be shared.
practiceSentences: Every classroom printer is networked to one server.
What becomes possible once a device is networked?
A networked device is reachable, which is its use and its risk.
The networked sensors reported the flood before anyone saw it.
Networked means connected; standalone means it works alone.

obligation.childMeaning: Something you are required to do by duty or agreement.
practiceSentences: The apprenticeship carries an obligation to complete two years.
What obligation does an employer owe a trainee?
An obligation binds whether or not you feel like it.
She met every obligation and resented half of them.
An obligation is owed; a choice is made.

onomatopoeia.childMeaning: A word that imitates the sound it names.
practiceSentences: Crackle, hiss and thud are all onomatopoeia.
Which onomatopoeia does the poet use for the rain?
Onomatopoeia lets a reader hear the scene, not just picture it.
The drum passage is built almost entirely from onomatopoeia.
Onomatopoeia differs between languages, which tells you it is not pure imitation.

open-source.childMeaning: Describing software whose code anyone may read and change.
practiceSentences: The tool is open-source, so anyone can inspect what it does.
Why does open-source matter for trusting a program?
Open-source is not the same as free of charge.
They chose an open-source encyclopedia over a closed one.
Open-source publishes the code; proprietary keeps it hidden.

optimise.childMeaning: To make something work as well as it possibly can.
practiceSentences: The signals were optimised for buses rather than cars.
What would you optimise first on this route?
To optimise is to choose what to make worse.
They optimised the timetable and lost the spare capacity.
Optimise means best for a stated purpose, so state the purpose.

organic.childMeaning: Grown without artificial chemicals, or to do with living things.
practiceSentences: Organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides.
Is organic always better for the land?
Organic farming uses more land for the same yield.
The word organic also means anything containing carbon.
Organic on a label is a legal claim, not a compliment.

originality.childMeaning: The quality of being new and not copied from anything.
practiceSentences: Originality is rarer than the word suggests.
What gives this proposal its originality?
Originality is not the same as never having been influenced.
The judges rewarded originality over polish.
Originality is being first; creativity is being able to be.

osmosis.childMeaning: The movement of water through a membrane towards the stronger solution.
practiceSentences: Osmosis moves water into the root without any pumping.
In which direction does osmosis carry the water here?
Osmosis needs a membrane that lets water through and not the dissolved substance.
Reverse osmosis is how some plants make drinking water from the sea.
People say they learned something by osmosis, which is a joke about the word.

paradox.childMeaning: A statement that seems to contradict itself yet holds a truth.
practiceSentences: The more you explain the joke, the less funny it is: that is a paradox.
Which paradox is the poem built around?
A paradox is not a mistake; it is a truth folded awkwardly.
She ended on a paradox and left the audience arguing.
A paradox seems contradictory; a contradiction simply is.

parody.childMeaning: An imitation of a style, made to be funny.
practiceSentences: The sketch was a parody of the evening news.
What is this parody actually imitating?
A parody has to copy well before it can mock.
Their parody of the advert was shared more widely than the advert.
A parody imitates a style; a caricature exaggerates a person.

participle.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept.
practiceSentences: In the torn label, torn is a past participle.
Which participle opens this sentence?
A participle can act as an adjective or help build a tense.
The present participle ends in -ing in every case.
A participle is a verb form doing a describing job.

percentile.childMeaning: A value below which a given percentage of results fall.
practiceSentences: Her time put her in the ninetieth percentile.
Which percentile marks the qualifying standard?
A percentile says where you stand, not how fast you are.
The fiftieth percentile is the median.
A percentile ranks; a percentage measures.

periodic.childMeaning: Happening at regular intervals, or arranged in repeating patterns.
practiceSentences: The system runs a periodic backup every night.
What periodic checks does this equipment need?
A periodic signal repeats itself at a fixed rate.
The periodic table arranges elements by repeating properties.
Periodic repeats on a schedule; occasional does not.

personality.childMeaning: The pattern of qualities that makes a person who they are.
practiceSentences: Her personality comes through in every letter she wrote.
How much of a personality is formed by early years?
Personality is what stays constant across very different rooms.
The twins shared a face and almost no personality.
Personality is how you are; character is how you act.

plausible.note: Meaning inherited from grade 8 and kept.
practiceSentences: The explanation is plausible and still needs testing.
Is that a plausible reason for the decline?
A plausible story is easier to believe than a true one.
She rejected the plausible answer and looked for evidence.
Plausible means it could be true; proven means it is.

pluralism.childMeaning: The principle that many different groups and beliefs can share one society.
pluralism.repitchedFrom: grade 5 unit 7. The meaning was pitched for a younger reader ('can live together well') and the sentences named Daniel, who is not in this grade's readings, and were set at 'circle time' - primary-school framing on a Grade 7 card. This grade meets pluralism beside secularism and internationalism, as a principle rather than a description of a nice street.
practiceSentences: Pluralism holds that disagreement is a permanent condition, not a fault to be fixed.
How does pluralism differ from simply tolerating a neighbour?
Pluralism asks a society to build rules that no single group writes.
Sana argued that the festival was pluralism in its most cheerful form.
Pluralism accepts many truths in public; it does not require you to hold them all.

predicate.childMeaning: The part of a sentence that says something about the subject.
practiceSentences: In the bus arrived late, arrived late is the predicate.
Which words form the predicate here?
A predicate always contains a verb.
She split each sentence into subject and predicate.
The subject names it; the predicate says what about it.

principled.childMeaning: Acting from firm beliefs about right and wrong.
practiceSentences: A principled refusal cost her the contract.
What makes a decision principled rather than convenient?
A principled stand is only tested when it costs something.
He was principled to the point of being difficult.
Principled means guided by principle; stubborn means guided by nothing.

probe.childMeaning: To investigate something closely, or an instrument for doing so.
