practiceSentences: The team probed the sediment for traces of the old shoreline.
What would you probe first?
To probe is to keep asking after the obvious answer.
She pushed the probe into the soil and read the temperature.
A probe investigates; a survey counts.

productivity.childMeaning: How much is produced for the effort or time put in.
practiceSentences: Productivity rose when the shifts were shortened.
How would you measure productivity in this job?
Productivity counts output against input, and both need defining.
Long hours and high productivity are not the same thing.
Productivity is a ratio; production is a total.

programmable.childMeaning: Able to be given instructions that change what it does.
practiceSentences: A programmable thermostat learns the week's pattern.
What makes this device programmable rather than merely adjustable?
A programmable machine can do a job nobody designed it for.
The programmable board cost less than the fixed one.
Programmable takes new instructions; automatic only repeats its own.

prologue.childMeaning: An opening section that comes before the main story.
practiceSentences: The prologue explains what happened a hundred years earlier.
Why does this book need a prologue at all?
A prologue sets the ground the story will stand on.
She read the prologue twice before beginning chapter one.
A prologue comes before; an epilogue comes after.

propaganda.note: Sentence 4 named Teacher Yasmin, who belongs to Grade 5. The set is otherwise squarely this unit's subject.
practiceSentences: The advertisement was really propaganda, sharing only the facts that suited the company.
A few leaders claimed the scientists were spreading propaganda to seize the forest.
How can a careful reader tell honest reporting apart from clever propaganda?
"Propaganda hides one side of the story," the teacher explained to the class.
I now check several sources so that propaganda cannot fool me into a bad choice.

proportionality.childMeaning: A fixed relationship in which one quantity scales with another.
practiceSentences: The graph shows proportionality between distance and time.
Is there proportionality across the whole range?
Proportionality means doubling one doubles the other.
The recipe relies on proportionality, so it scales to any number.
Proportionality is a constant ratio; correlation need not be.

quadratic.childMeaning: Describing an expression in which the highest power is two.
practiceSentences: A quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
Which term makes this equation quadratic?
A quadratic graph is a curve, never a straight line.
She solved the quadratic by completing the square.
Quadratic means squared; linear means to the first power.

qualification.note: The inherited set held four sentences, not five. Kept otherwise - this is a word-building card, whose examples need not sit in the unit's subject.
practiceSentences: A recognised qualification in accounting opened doors that years of unrecorded experience could not.
Which qualification would help most if you wanted to work as a wildlife photographer?
"Experience matters," said the recruiter, "but without the right qualification your application stops at the first desk."
I plan to earn a lifeguarding qualification next summer so I can work at the community pool.
A qualification is also a limit added to a claim, as in a qualified apology.

qualify.childMeaning: To add a limit to a statement so it is not too broad.
practiceSentences: Qualify the claim before somebody else does it for you.
How would you qualify this conclusion?
To qualify a statement is to make it defensible, not to weaken it.
She qualified every finding with the size of the sample.
Qualify also means to become eligible, as for a competition.

quantifier.childMeaning: A word that tells you how much or how many.
practiceSentences: Many, few and several are quantifiers.
Which quantifier fits an uncountable noun?
A quantifier answers how much before anything is described.
English uses different quantifiers for countable and uncountable nouns.
A quantifier counts; a determiner points.

random.childMeaning: Chosen with no pattern, so every outcome is equally likely.
practiceSentences: A random sample gives everyone the same chance of being picked.
Is that selection random or merely unplanned?
Random does not mean haphazard: it has to be arranged.
Lanes were assigned at random before the heats.
Random means no pattern; arbitrary means no reason.

rank.childMeaning: To place things in order according to their value or size.
practiceSentences: Rank these five options before you argue for any of them.
How would you rank the candidates on evidence alone?
Ranking forces a choice that listing avoids.
She ranked the tasks and the timetable wrote itself.
To rank is to order; to rate is to score each one separately.

rational.note: Inherited from grade 8 and kept, with one change. Sentence 5 read '...though I admit the bus's warmth sways me in January' - a cold January, which is a temperate-climate assumption on a card in an East African course. The rest of the set is about flood plans and water use, which belongs here.
practiceSentences: Panic spreads quickly, so leaders must stay rational when plans go wrong.
A rational flood plan weighs the cost of barriers against the price of doing nothing.
Is it rational to plant thirsty lawns in a town that faces water shortages every summer?
"Stay rational," said the chairperson gently; "anger fills the room but empties the budget."
I try to make rational choices about water, though the longest shower is always tempting.

reactant.childMeaning: A substance that is used up in a chemical reaction.
practiceSentences: The reactant is consumed; the catalyst is not.
Which reactant runs out first here?
A reaction stops when one reactant is exhausted.
She measured each reactant before mixing anything.
Reactants go in; products come out.

reassess.childMeaning: To judge something again in the light of new information.
practiceSentences: The result made them reassess the whole approach.
When would you reassess this decision?
To reassess is not to admit defeat; it is to use what arrived late.
She reassessed the plan and kept three quarters of it.
Reassessing regularly is cheaper than being wrong for a year.

recognition.childMeaning: The act of knowing something again, or of publicly acknowledging it.
practiceSentences: Face recognition unlocks the phone in less than a second.
What recognition did the reporters receive for the investigation?
Recognition of a pattern is faster than reasoning about it.
The paper won recognition it had not sought.
Recognition can mean identifying something, or honouring somebody.

reconstruct.childMeaning: To build something again from the evidence that remains.
practiceSentences: Historians reconstruct a household from a list and a will.
How would you reconstruct this journey from three letters?
To reconstruct is to argue, however carefully it is done.
They reconstructed the market square from a single photograph.
Reconstructing the past means choosing what to leave out.

refrain.childMeaning: A line or group of lines repeated through a poem or song.
practiceSentences: The refrain returns at the end of every verse.
How many times does the refrain come round?
A refrain lets a crowd join in without learning the whole song.
The refrain changes one word each time, which is the point.
A refrain is repetition with a purpose.

refute.childMeaning: To prove that a statement is wrong.
practiceSentences: One counterexample was enough to refute the rule.
What evidence would refute this claim?
To refute is to disprove, not merely to deny.
He refuted the argument and conceded the conclusion.
Refute needs evidence; reject needs only an opinion.

reinterpret.childMeaning: To understand something in a new way.
practiceSentences: Each generation reinterprets the same founding story.
How would you reinterpret this letter knowing who wrote it?
To reinterpret is not to rewrite; the evidence stays put.
The exhibition reinterprets objects the museum has held for a century.
History gets reinterpreted more often than it gets discovered.

rephrase.childMeaning: To say or write something again in different words.
practiceSentences: Rephrase the question if nobody answers it.
How would you rephrase this for a younger reader?
Rephrasing something you half understand shows you which half.
She rephrased the offer and it suddenly sounded fair.
To rephrase is to change the words; to paraphrase is to compress them too.

replicate.childMeaning: To repeat something exactly so the result can be checked.
practiceSentences: Another team could not replicate the finding.
How would you replicate this study on a different river?
A result nobody can replicate is not yet a result.
They replicated the count three times in one week.
To replicate is to repeat the method; to copy is to repeat the answer.

representation.childMeaning: The way something or someone is shown or described.
representation.repitchedFrom: the inherited meaning joined two senses with a semicolon - 'a way of showing or describing something, like a picture or a model; also, speaking on behalf of others'. In a unit about media the depiction sense is the one that matters; the speaking-for sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: The film's representation of the town annoyed everyone who lives there.
What representation of young people does this article offer?
A representation is always a choice about what to leave out.
The mural was a colourful representation of the many cultures within our school.
Representation also means speaking or acting on behalf of others.

republic.childMeaning: A country whose head of state is elected, not born to the role.
practiceSentences: The country became a republic in nineteen sixty.
What is the difference between a republic and a monarchy?
A republic elects its head of state; a monarchy inherits one.
The new republic wrote its constitution in eighteen months.
A republic is a form of state, not a guarantee of freedom.

rhetoric.childMeaning: The art of using language to persuade.
practiceSentences: The speech was fine rhetoric and thin on evidence.
What rhetoric does this headline use?
Rhetoric is a skill, and a skill can be used either way.
She studied rhetoric to become harder to persuade.
Rhetoric is the craft of persuasion; propaganda is persuasion with the other side removed.

robust.childMeaning: Strong, and able to hold up under pressure or scrutiny.
practiceSentences: The finding is robust across three different seasons.
Is this conclusion robust enough to publish?
A robust result survives being tested by somebody hostile.
Their robust defence conceded twice in twenty matches.
Robust withstands; rigid resists until it breaks.

safeguarding.childMeaning: Protecting people, especially children, from harm.
practiceSentences: Safeguarding rules govern every school trip.
What safeguarding does a busy crossing require?
Safeguarding is a duty before it is a procedure.
The council reviewed its safeguarding after the near miss.
Safeguarding protects people; security protects property.

sampling.childMeaning: Choosing part of a group to learn about the whole.
practiceSentences: Sampling every tenth runner gave a fair picture.
What sampling method did the study use?
Careless sampling produces confident nonsense.
Random sampling avoids the choices a person would make.
Sampling saves time; bad sampling wastes everything after it.

sanction.childMeaning: A penalty imposed to make a country or person obey.
practiceSentences: The sanctions were lifted after the agreement was signed.
What sanction would actually change this behaviour?
A sanction is meant to cost more than the behaviour is worth.
Trade sanctions hurt the people before they reach the government.
Sanction is its own opposite: it also means to give official approval.

satirical.childMeaning: Using humour to expose and criticise something.
practiceSentences: The satirical column is the most read page in the paper.
Is this piece satirical or simply rude?
A satirical article attacks a target, not merely a mood.
Satirical writing needs its readers to know what is being mocked.
Satirical mocks in order to criticise; comic only wants a laugh.

scansion.childMeaning: The marking out of a poem's rhythm, beat by beat.
practiceSentences: Scansion shows where the stresses actually fall.
What does scansion reveal about this opening line?
Scansion turns a feeling about rhythm into something you can point at.
She practised scansion by tapping the beats on the desk.
Scansion measures the metre; it does not create it.

scatter.childMeaning: A graph that plots two measurements against each other.
practiceSentences: A scatter graph shows every athlete as one point.
What does the scatter tell you about the relationship?
A scatter plot reveals a pattern a table hides.
The points scatter widely, so the link is weak.
Scatter also means to throw about, which is what the points seem to do.

secularism.childMeaning: Keeping religion separate from the running of the state.
practiceSentences: Secularism keeps the state neutral between beliefs.
Does secularism mean a country has no religion?
Secularism is about the state, not about what anyone privately believes.
The constitution established secularism in its first article.
Secularism separates religion from government; atheism rejects religion itself.

selection.childMeaning: The process by which some living things survive to breed and others do not.
practiceSentences: Natural selection acts on variation that already exists.
What pressure is driving selection on this island?
Selection does not plan; it only keeps what survives.
Over generations, selection made the beaks measurably deeper.
Selection also means simply choosing, which is what makes the term easy to misread.
selection.note: Sentence 2 read 'What is being selected for on this island?' - `selected` is the verb, not the noun this card teaches. Same call as profitable, adjustment and tessellate before it.

self-concept.childMeaning: The idea a person holds of who they are.
practiceSentences: A self-concept is built from what others reflect back.
How does moving country change a self-concept?
A self-concept can be accurate or badly out of date.
His self-concept shifted the year he began to teach.
Self-concept is the picture; self-esteem is how you feel about it.

self-efficacy.childMeaning: Your belief that you can do what a task requires.
practiceSentences: Self-efficacy grows from small successes, not from encouragement.
How does one hard exam affect self-efficacy?
Self-efficacy is about a particular task, not about yourself in general.
Her self-efficacy in mathematics rose the term she stopped guessing.
Self-efficacy is what you believe you can do; confidence is how you feel.

semantic.childMeaning: To do with the meaning of words.
practiceSentences: The disagreement was semantic: they meant different things by fair.
What semantic difference separates these two words?
A semantic field groups words that share a subject.
She traced the semantic shift of the word across two centuries.
Semantic is about meaning; syntactic is about arrangement.

significance.childMeaning: The importance of something, or how much it matters.
practiceSentences: The significance of the result was clear only after the second trial.
What is the significance of this date in the file?
Significance is not the same as size: a tiny change can matter enormously.
She explained the significance of the missing metadata.
In statistics, significance means a result is unlikely to be chance.

simultaneous.childMeaning: Happening or being solved at the same time.
practiceSentences: Simultaneous equations are solved together, not one after the other.
What makes these two equations simultaneous?
Two simultaneous equations share a solution that fits both.
The simultaneous broadcasts reached four countries at once.
Simultaneous means at once; consecutive means one then the next.

socialisation.childMeaning: The way people learn the customs and rules of their society.
practiceSentences: Socialisation begins long before school does.
What part does family play in socialisation?
Socialisation teaches what is normal before it teaches what is right.
The study compared socialisation in two neighbouring villages.
Socialisation is learning to belong, and it is rarely explicit.

socialism.childMeaning: A system in which key industries and services are owned by the public.
socialism.note: Sentences 1 and 2 were the same sentence - the community paying together for hospitals and schools, and the government providing services like hospitals. The grade 6 meaning also said the government 'controls important things like schools and hospitals', which describes public services rather than the system.
practiceSentences: Under socialism, key industries are publicly rather than privately owned.
How does socialism try to reduce the gap between the richest and poorest citizens?
Socialism and a welfare state are not the same thing, though they often travel together.
Supporters of socialism argue that shared hospitals and schools protect families during a serious crisis.
I compared socialism with capitalism to understand how each system organises a country's economy.

solidarity.childMeaning: Standing together with others who share a cause or a hardship.
practiceSentences: The whole market closed for an hour in solidarity.
What does solidarity cost the person offering it?
Solidarity is support that carries a risk; sympathy need not.
Jamal wore the ribbon in solidarity with the striking drivers.
Solidarity is a verb pretending to be a noun.

soliloquy.childMeaning: A speech in which a character alone on stage thinks aloud.
practiceSentences: The soliloquy lets the audience hear what nobody else may.
Where does the soliloquy fall in the play?
A soliloquy is spoken alone; an aside is spoken past the others.
His soliloquy runs to forty lines and changes the whole play.
A soliloquy reveals a mind; a dialogue reveals a relationship.

sophisticated.note: All four inherited sentences were about a city's transport - traffic signals, flood barriers, a ticketing app - which is unit 4's subject, and the set held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: The mill uses a sophisticated system to recover its own water.
How sophisticated does a dyeing process need to be?
A sophisticated method is not automatically a better one.
Her sophisticated grasp of the supply chain came from a summer's work.
Sophisticated means highly developed, and once meant something closer to corrupted.

speaker.childMeaning: The voice a poem is written in, which is not the poet.
practiceSentences: The speaker of the poem is a soldier, not the poet herself.
What do we learn about the speaker from the first line?
The speaker is a character the poet invents, sometimes unlike them entirely.
Confusing the speaker with the poet is the commonest mistake in essays.
Speaker also means anybody talking, which is why this use has to be taught.

specialisation.childMeaning: Concentrating on one narrow area of work or study.
practiceSentences: Her specialisation is the security of medical devices.
What specialisation would you choose in computing?
Specialisation buys depth and costs breadth.
Early specialisation can close doors you have not seen yet.
Specialisation narrows on purpose; a general training does not.

stability.childMeaning: The quality of staying steady and not changing unexpectedly.
practiceSentences: The system ran for a year without losing stability.
What threatens the stability of this network?
Stability is boring, which is how you know it is working.
They chose stability over the newest version.
Stability resists change; rigidity cannot accept it.

statistical.childMeaning: Based on the collecting and study of numerical data.
practiceSentences: The claim rests on a statistical difference, not a visible one.
Is this a statistical result or a single good day?
A statistical finding says how likely a pattern is to be chance.
The federation published a statistical review of the season.
Statistical means from the numbers; anecdotal means from a story.

statute.childMeaning: A law formally written down and passed by a parliament.
practiceSentences: The right of way is protected by statute.
Which statute covers noise at night?
A statute is written law; a custom is not.
The statute was passed in nineteen seventy and never amended.
A statute is the law itself; a policy is how a body applies it.

stigma.childMeaning: A mark of shame unfairly attached to a person or group.
practiceSentences: The stigma kept people from asking for the help they needed.
What stigma still surrounds this subject?
A stigma survives long after the belief behind it has gone.
Campaigners worked to remove the stigma rather than the word.
A stigma is attached by others; shame is felt inside.

subjective.childMeaning: Based on personal feelings rather than on facts.
practiceSentences: A review is subjective and should say so.
Is that judgement subjective or can it be tested?
A subjective opinion is not thereby worthless.
She separated the subjective paragraphs from the reported ones.
Subjective comes from the person; objective from the thing.

subjunctive.childMeaning: A verb form used for wishes, suggestions and unreal situations.
practiceSentences: In if I were you, were is subjunctive.
Where would a subjunctive be used in this sentence?
The subjunctive survives in English mostly in set phrases.
She used the subjunctive and it sounded unexpectedly formal.
The subjunctive describes what is wished for, not what is.

subordinating.childMeaning: Describing a word that makes one clause depend on another.
practiceSentences: Because, although and unless are subordinating conjunctions.
Which subordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A subordinating conjunction turns a clause into a part of another.
Journalists use subordinating clauses to bury what they would rather not stress.
Subordinating makes one clause depend; coordinating joins equals.

substantiate.childMeaning: To support a claim with evidence.
practiceSentences: Substantiate each assertion or remove it.
What would substantiate this figure?
To substantiate is to show the working, not to repeat the claim.
The article failed to substantiate its most quoted sentence.
Substantiate provides evidence; assert provides none.

substitution.childMeaning: Replacing a word or phrase with a shorter one to avoid repeating it.
practiceSentences: In I have a laptop and she has one too, one is a substitution.
Which word is doing the substitution here?
Substitution replaces; ellipsis removes altogether.
Careful substitution keeps a paragraph from repeating a long noun.
Words like one, do and so are the commonest substitutions in English.

subtext.childMeaning: The meaning underneath what is actually said.
practiceSentences: The subtext of the statement was that nobody would be blamed.
What is the subtext of this apology?
Subtext is what a careful reader hears and a quick one misses.
She read the subtext before she finished the first paragraph.
The text is what is written; the subtext is what is meant.

sustainability.childMeaning: Meeting today's needs without using up what later generations will need.
sustainability.repitchedFrom: the inherited meaning opened 'Sustainability means using resources carefully...' - restating its own headword. All four of its sentences were about a river and a tree-planting programme, which is unit 5's subject, and one named Teacher Yasmin, who belongs to Grade 5. The set also held four sentences, not five.
practiceSentences: Sustainability in clothing is measured in wears, not in purchases.
What would sustainability actually require of this factory?
Sustainability asks what happens if everyone does it, for ever.
The brand's sustainability claims covered the cotton and not the dye.
Sustainability is a test a practice either passes or fails over time.

syntactic.childMeaning: To do with how words are arranged in a sentence.
practiceSentences: The syntactic structure changes where the emphasis falls.
What syntactic feature makes this sentence hard to read?
A syntactic error breaks the sentence; a lexical one only misnames.
The poet's syntactic inversions slow the reader deliberately.
Syntactic concerns arrangement; semantic concerns meaning.

syntax.childMeaning: The arrangement of words to make a well-formed sentence.
practiceSentences: The syntax is correct even where the meaning is not.
What does the poet's unusual syntax achieve?
Syntax decides what a sentence can mean before any word is chosen.
Inverted syntax slows a reader down, which may be the point.
Syntax is the order; semantics is the meaning.

tariff.childMeaning: A tax charged on goods coming into a country.
practiceSentences: A tariff on imported cloth protects local weavers and raises prices.
Who ends up paying the tariff?
A tariff is paid at the border, and passed along afterwards.
The tariff was lifted and the price fell within a month.
A tariff taxes imports; a subsidy pays producers.

tentative.childMeaning: Not certain, and open to being changed.
practiceSentences: The conclusion is tentative until a second season confirms it.
Is that a tentative finding or a settled one?
A tentative claim is honest about how much it knows.
They published a tentative figure and invited correction.
Tentative means held lightly, not held weakly.

theorem.childMeaning: A statement in mathematics that has been proved from other truths.
practiceSentences: The theorem holds for every right-angled triangle.
Which theorem would you use here?
A theorem is proved once and then relied on for ever.
She quoted the theorem rather than reproving it.
A theorem is proved; a conjecture is only believed.

toxin.childMeaning: A poisonous substance, especially one made by a living thing.
practiceSentences: Some dyes release a toxin into the river below the mill.
Which toxin does this process leave behind?
A toxin harms in small amounts, which is what makes it one.
Strictly, a toxin is produced by an organism; a poison need not be.
The toxin was traced to a single discharge pipe.

tragedy.childMeaning: A play in which the main character is brought down, often by their own flaw.
tragedy.repitchedFrom: grade 8 unit 9: 'A serious story or event, often ending in sadness or loss.' That folds the dramatic FORM into any sad happening, and on a capstone card beside soliloquy, allusion and paradox the form is what the learner needs. The everyday sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: A tragedy turns on a flaw in the hero rather than on bad luck.
What flaw brings this tragedy about?
A tragedy ends badly by design, and the audience sees it coming.
The play is a tragedy because the fall could have been avoided.
Tragedy also means any terrible event, which is the everyday use.

transformation.note: Meaning inherited from grade 6 and kept - it is precise and needs no re-pitching.
practiceSentences: The transformation of the draft between March and June was total.
What transformation does the character undergo?
A transformation changes the nature of a thing, not only its surface.
Her transformation as a writer began with cutting adjectives.
In mathematics a transformation moves or resizes a shape.

transitive.childMeaning: Describing a verb that takes an object.
practiceSentences: In she carried the pack, carried is transitive.
Which verb in this sentence is transitive?
A transitive verb needs something to act on.
Many verbs are transitive in one sentence and not in the next.
A transitive verb takes an object; an intransitive one does not.

unemployment.childMeaning: The state of wanting paid work and not having it.
practiceSentences: Unemployment among school leavers rose for a third year.
What causes unemployment in a town with one industry?
Unemployment counts those looking for work, not everyone without it.
The figures hid unemployment behind part-time contracts.
Unemployment is measured; the experience of it is not.

union.childMeaning: An organisation of workers formed to protect their interests.
practiceSentences: The garment workers formed a union after the third wage cut.
What can a union do that one worker cannot?
A union bargains for many so that no one bargains alone.
The union negotiated a safety inspection into the contract.
Union also means the joining of two things into one.

urbanisation.childMeaning: The growth of towns and cities as people move into them.
practiceSentences: Urbanisation doubled the city's population in twenty years.
What drives urbanisation in this region?
Urbanisation arrives faster than the housing built for it.
The map traces urbanisation along the coast road.
Urbanisation is the movement; a city is the result.

vaccination.childMeaning: Giving a vaccine so the body can build immunity in advance.
practiceSentences: Vaccination is required before travelling to some tournaments.
Why does vaccination protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
Vaccination trains the immune system without the illness.
The squad completed its vaccination two months before the games.
A vaccine is the substance; vaccination is the act of giving it.

validation.childMeaning: Checking that something is correct or meets its requirements.
practiceSentences: Form validation catches the missing digit before the form is sent.
What validation does this data go through?
Validation checks the input; verification checks the result.
Without validation, one wrong date corrupted the whole export.
Validation also means having your feelings acknowledged, which is a different use.

validity.childMeaning: The quality of being well founded and able to stand up to testing.
practiceSentences: The validity of the conclusion rests on one unchecked figure.
How would you test the validity of this argument?
Validity is about the reasoning; truth is about the world.
An argument can have validity and still reach a false conclusion.
A ticket has validity too, which is the everyday use of the word.

variability.childMeaning: How much something varies from one measurement to the next.
practiceSentences: The variability between the two seasons made the average useless.
What variability would you expect in this data?
High variability hides a pattern that a mean pretends is there.
She reported the variability alongside the average, as she should.
Variability is how much it changes; a variable is what changes.

vector.childMeaning: A quantity that has both a size and a direction.
practiceSentences: Velocity is a vector; speed is not.
Which vector describes the wind this morning?
A vector needs a direction or it is only a number.
The two vectors added to almost nothing.
A vector is also anything that carries a disease from place to place.

weigh.childMeaning: To consider the importance of things against each other.
weigh.repitchedFrom: grade 4 unit 1: 'To find out how heavy something is.' - the physical sense, three grades below, on a card among appraise, rank and reassess. Here you weigh options rather than objects. The physical sense is named in the fifth sentence.
practiceSentences: Weigh the cost of training against the years it buys you.
How do you weigh a certain small gain against an uncertain large one?
To weigh two options is to admit both have something in them.
She weighed the offer carefully and turned it down.
Weigh also means to measure how heavy something is.

yield.childMeaning: The amount a process or a piece of land produces.
practiceSentences: Organic cotton gives a lower yield per hectare.
What yield does this dye process actually return?
A high yield tells you nothing about what it cost.
The yield fell in the second season and nobody knew why.
Yield also means to give way, which is a different word doing double duty.
